Each Insurer Party shall provide written confirmation to Calderwood & Harkness LLP of the initiation of its wire transfer no later than two (2) business days prior to the Payment Deadline. Each Insurer Party shall be severally, and not jointly, liable for its respective share of the Settlement Amount as set forth in Section 2.2. No Insurer Party shall be liable, in whole or in part, for the payment obligation of any other Insurer Party. The payment by each Insurer Party of its respective share shall fully discharge that Insurer Party\'s financial obligations under this Agreement regardless of whether any other Insurer Party pays or fails to pay its respective share.

**Section 2.4** *Late Payment.* In the event that any Insurer Party fails to remit its respective share of the Settlement Amount on or before the Payment Deadline, the unpaid amount shall bear interest at the rate of twelve percent (12%) per annum, or the maximum rate permitted under applicable Florida law, whichever is less, computed from the day immediately following the Payment Deadline until the date upon which such payment is received in full. The accrual of interest under this Section 2.4 shall not constitute a waiver of any other rights or remedies available to VHG at law or in equity for any Insurer Party\'s failure to timely make payment, including the right to seek specific performance or other equitable relief.

**Section 2.5** *Tax Treatment.* Each Party shall be solely responsible for its own tax obligations, if any, arising from the settlement or the payments made pursuant to this Agreement. No Party makes any representation or warranty to any other Party regarding the tax treatment or tax consequences of the Settlement Amount or any portion thereof. VHG acknowledges and agrees that no Insurer Party, nor any agent, employee, or counsel of any Insurer Party, has provided or is providing any tax advice to VHG with respect to the Settlement Amount or any portion thereof. The Parties agree that VHG will report the Settlement Amount as proceeds from an insurance recovery for business-interruption losses for applicable tax purposes. Nothing in this Section 2.5 shall be construed as tax advice, and each Party is encouraged to consult with its own qualified tax advisors regarding the tax treatment of the Settlement Amount.
**[ARTICLE III --- DISMISSAL OF LITIGATION]{.underline}**

**Section 3.1** *Stipulation of Dismissal.* Within ten (10) business days following receipt by VHG (through the trust account of Calderwood & Harkness LLP) of the full Settlement Amount from all Insurer Parties, the Parties shall jointly execute and file a Joint Stipulation of Dismissal with Prejudice of all claims, counterclaims, cross-claims, and affirmative defenses in the Litigation, Case No. 2022-CA-031547, in the Eleventh Judicial Circuit of Florida, in and for Miami-Dade County, before the Honorable Catherine Embry, Circuit Judge. The Joint Stipulation of Dismissal with Prejudice shall provide for the dismissal of all claims and counterclaims asserted by any Party in the Litigation with prejudice to their re-filing and shall be in substantially the form attached hereto as Exhibit B, or in such other form as shall be mutually agreed upon by the Parties through their respective counsel.

**Section 3.2** *Costs and Fees.* Except as otherwise expressly provided in this Agreement, each Party shall bear its own costs, expenses, and attorneys\' fees incurred in connection with the Litigation and the negotiation, preparation, and execution of this Agreement. Without limiting the generality of the foregoing, VHG\'s engagement of Calderwood & Harkness LLP as its litigation counsel and the fees, costs, and expenses incurred by VHG in connection therewith are solely VHG\'s responsibility, and no Insurer Party shall bear any liability for any portion of such fees, costs, or expenses.

**Section 3.3** *Withdrawal of Pending Motions.* Upon the filing of the Joint Stipulation of Dismissal with Prejudice in the Litigation, all pending motions in the Litigation shall be deemed withdrawn and rendered moot, including without limitation: (a) VHG\'s Motion for Partial Summary Judgment Regarding the Applicability of the Named-Windstorm Sub-Limit to Business-Interruption Losses, filed on November 1, 2023; and (b) the Cross-Motion for Partial Summary Judgment filed by Ironclad, Pinnacle, Montclair, and Sovereign Re on November 15, 2023. The Parties agree to cooperate in informing the Court that such motions are withdrawn and need not be adjudicated.
**[ARTICLE IV --- MUTUAL RELEASE]{.underline}**

**Section 4.1** *Release by VHG.* Effective upon VHG\'s receipt of the full Settlement Amount from all Insurer Parties, VHG, on behalf of itself and all VHG Parties, hereby irrevocably and unconditionally releases, acquits, and forever discharges each and every Insurer Party, and each of their respective parents, subsidiaries, affiliates, officers, directors, employees, agents (including, without limitation, Arbor Claims Services LLC and its employees, agents, and representatives, including specifically Denise Whitford), underwriters, reinsurers, predecessors, successors, assigns, and legal counsel (including, without limitation, Fendowell Rourke & Stanton LLP and its attorneys Gregory Stanton, Meredith Liang, and Colin Ashford; and Delvecchio & Kraus LLP and its attorneys Patricia Kraus and Raymond Cho), from any and all Claims of every kind and nature whatsoever, whether at law or in equity, whether known or unknown, suspected or unsuspected, asserted or unasserted, fixed or contingent, matured or unmatured, accrued or not yet accrued, arising out of or relating to the Hurricane Callista Losses and/or the Policies (collectively, the \"Released Claims\"). This release includes, without limitation, all claims for breach of contract, breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, statutory bad faith under Section 624.155 of the Florida Statutes, common-law bad faith, declaratory judgment, extra-contractual damages, consequential damages, statutory penalties, punitive damages, attorneys\' fees, pre-judgment and post-judgment interest, costs of litigation, and any and all other relief of any kind or nature whatsoever that was or could have been asserted in the Litigation or in any other action or proceeding.

**Section 4.2** *Release by Insurer Parties.* Effective upon payment of the full Settlement Amount by all Insurer Parties to VHG, each Insurer Party, on behalf of itself and its respective parents, subsidiaries, affiliates, officers, directors, employees, agents, underwriters, reinsurers, predecessors, successors, and assigns, hereby irrevocably and unconditionally releases, acquits, and forever discharges VHG and all VHG Parties, including, without limitation, VHG\'s officers (specifically Marcus Ellsworth, Diane Calder, Nathaniel Driscoll, and Sandra Pellegrini), directors, employees, agents, representatives, and legal counsel (including, without limitation, Calderwood & Harkness LLP and its attorneys Elaine Forsythe, Howard Bellamy, Tiffany Rosenthal, and Andrew Fitzpatrick), from any and all Claims of every kind and nature whatsoever, whether at law or in equity, whether known or unknown, suspected or unsuspected, asserted or unasserted, fixed or contingent, matured or unmatured, accrued or not yet accrued, arising out of or relating to the Hurricane Callista Losses and/or the Policies. This release includes, without limitation, any and all claims, counterclaims, or defenses that were or could have been asserted by any Insurer Party in the Litigation or in any other action or proceeding relating to the Hurricane Callista Losses and/or the Policies.

**Section 4.3** *Scope of Release.* The releases set forth in Sections 4.1 and 4.2 of this Agreement are intended to be as broad and comprehensive as permitted by law and extend to all Claims, whether known or unknown, suspected or unsuspected, disclosed or undisclosed, matured or unmatured, accrued or not yet accrued, that exist as of the Effective Date and that arise from, relate to, or are in any way connected with the Hurricane Callista Losses and/or the Policies. Each Party expressly, knowingly, and voluntarily waives any and all rights it may have under any statute, regulation, or common-law principle of any jurisdiction---including, but not limited to, Section 1542 of the California Civil Code and any analogous provision of Florida law or the law of any other jurisdiction---that would otherwise limit the scope of this release to claims known or suspected at the time of execution of this Agreement. Each Party acknowledges and understands that it may discover facts different from or in addition to those it now knows or believes to be true with respect to the Released Claims, and that the releases set forth herein shall remain in full force and effect notwithstanding such discovery.

**Section 4.4** *Carve-Out --- Enforcement of This Agreement.* Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in this Article IV, nothing in this Agreement shall release any Party from its obligations, covenants, representations, or warranties set forth in this Agreement. Each Party expressly retains the right to enforce the terms and conditions of this Agreement, to seek specific performance of any obligation hereunder, and to pursue any available remedies for breach of this Agreement.

**Section 4.5** *No Release of Third-Party Claims.* The releases set forth in this Article IV do not extend to, and shall not be construed to release or affect, any claims VHG may have against third parties that are not signatories to this Agreement, including but not limited to Tidewater Risk Advisors LLC, or any other broker, agent, or consultant. Similarly, the releases set forth in this Article IV do not extend to, and shall not be construed to release or affect, any claims by any Insurer Party against third parties that are not signatories to this Agreement, including but not limited to any claims for contribution, indemnification, or subrogation against non-party third parties.
**[ARTICLE V --- NO ADMISSION OF LIABILITY]{.underline}**

**Section 5.1** *No Admission.* This Agreement and the settlement reflected herein are the result of a compromise of disputed claims and shall not be construed as an admission of liability, fault, wrongdoing, or the validity or invalidity of any claim or defense by any Party. Without limiting the generality of the foregoing:

> \(a\) No Insurer Party admits or concedes that any coverage was owed to VHG under any of the Policies with respect to the Hurricane Callista Losses, that any denial or reservation of rights was improper, unfounded, or made in bad faith, or that any Policy provision, including the named-windstorm sub-limit, the flood exclusion, the concurrent-causation provision, or any other provision, was inapplicable to VHG\'s claim.

> \(b\) VHG does not admit or concede that its claim for business-interruption losses was overstated, exaggerated, or otherwise unsupported, that it failed to mitigate its losses, or that any amount less than its full claimed losses was the proper measure of recovery under the Policies.

> \(c\) This Agreement, and any of its terms, provisions, or the fact of settlement, may not be offered, received, or admitted in evidence in any action, suit, or other proceeding of any kind or nature as an admission, concession, or evidence of liability, fault, wrongdoing, or the invalidity of any claim or defense by any Party, except in an action to enforce the terms of this Agreement.
**[ARTICLE VI --- CONFIDENTIALITY]{.underline}**

Line 537: The early and aggressive pursuit of Suncoast Room Management Inc.\'s financial records was critical to the successful prosecution of this matter. Line 547: The lesson for future franchise matters is that franchisor clients should be advised to systematically cultivate and protect whistleblower relationships. Line 553: For future matters, where pre-litigation audit work is performed by a different firm than the retained litigation expert, engagement terms should be structured from the outset to facilitate coordination, and the preliminary audit engagement should be scoped with an awareness that its findings may become exhibits in subsequent litigation.

Line 559: Before the summary-judgment ruling, Coastal Palms maintained a negotiating posture anchored in its contention that the GRR definition was ambiguous and that a reasonable jury could find in its favor on liability. Line 561: The investment in summary-judgment briefing --- which was substantial in both hours and effort --- was fully justified by the result. Line 567: The settlement structure directly addressed this concern. The \$25 million cash payment at closing provided immediate, certain recovery. The security interest in eight (8) unencumbered hotel properties --- valued at \$71.2 million in the aggregate --- provides collateral support for the \$62.5 million in structured payments that is not subordinate to Ironclad\'s liens. The personal guaranties from Brecker and Prescott provide additional recovery backstops, although the individual net worth of each guarantor was not independently verified.
Line 569: The lesson for future matters is that collectibility analysis must be conducted early in the litigation and revisited periodically. The availability (or unavailability) of unencumbered assets should drive both the settlement strategy and the structuring of any settlement consideration.
Line 573: The franchise surrender of fourteen (14) properties, while not reflected as a dollar amount in the \$87.5 million headline settlement figure, represents significant strategic value to Verimark. The franchise-surrender component was, in many respects, as important to Verimark from a brand-protection perspective as the monetary recovery.
Line 575: Additionally, the Enhanced Audit Protocol applicable to the eight (8) retained properties --- including quarterly audits, real-time POS integration, and franchisee-funded audit costs for five years --- provides Verimark with ongoing visibility into Coastal Palms\' revenue reporting that it did not previously have, substantially reducing the risk of future noncompliance.

Under Florida law, a liquidated-damages provision is enforceable only if the stipulated amount is a reasonable forecast of just compensation for the harm caused by the breach and the harm is of a kind that is difficult or impossible to accurately estimate at the time of contracting. *See Lefemine v. Baron*, 573 So. 2d 326 (Fla. 1991). A liquidated-damages provision that functions as a penalty --- rather than a reasonable pre-estimate of loss --- is unenforceable.

Line 583: Had the liquidated-damages claim been struck, Verimark\'s remaining damages would have consisted of the \$16.095 million in direct underpayments and the \$28.4 million in contractual late-payment interest, for a total of approximately \$44.5 million --- well below the \$87.5 million settlement. matches.line: **TO:** Matter File --- *Verimark Hospitality Group Inc. v. Coastal Palms Franchise Holdings LLC et al.*

The purpose of this memorandum is to memorialize the final disposition of the above-referenced matter, provide a comprehensive summary of the engagement from inception through closing, document the financial outcomes of the litigation --- including fees, costs, and the terms of the settlement achieved on behalf of the client --- capture key learnings and practice points for the benefit of the firm, and establish file-retention instructions in accordance with Calderwood & Harkness LLP\'s Document Retention Policy. This memorandum is intended to serve as the definitive internal record of the matter for future reference by firm attorneys, the conflicts department, and firm management.

The matter was formally closed on April 26, 2024, upon the filing and entry of the Joint Stipulation of Dismissal with Prejudice in Case No. 1021-00006 before the Honorable Richard M. Calloway, Circuit Judge, Circuit Court of the 17th Judicial Circuit in and for Broward County, Florida. All substantive obligations of Calderwood & Harkness LLP under the engagement letter dated March 4, 2022, as amended, have been fully performed, and the final invoice for legal services rendered in connection with this matter has been transmitted to the client.

**1. Client. Verimark Hospitality Group Inc.** (\"Verimark\" or \"VHG\") is a Delaware corporation publicly traded on the Nasdaq Stock Market under the ticker symbol VHMK. Verimark is headquartered at 2400 East Las Olas Boulevard, Suite 3100, Fort Lauderdale, Florida 33301. For fiscal year 2021 --- the most recent full fiscal year preceding the commencement of this litigation --- Verimark reported consolidated revenue of approximately \$1.42 billion, of which its franchise segment contributed approximately \$218 million. Verimark operates and franchises approximately 340 branded hotel properties under three primary flags --- Verimark Suites, Verimark Select, and Verimark Grand --- located predominantly across the southeastern United States.
> • **Renata Solis-Vega**, Senior Vice President and General Counsel --- principal point of contact for all legal strategy, settlement authority, and privilege-related matters.
> • **Martin Holcomb**, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer --- primary contact for financial matters, fee and cost approvals, budget discussions, and settlement economics.

> • **Deidre Langston**, Senior Vice President, Franchise Operations --- primary contact for operational matters, franchise compliance, property-level data, and post-settlement monitoring of franchise-surrender and enhanced-audit obligations.

**(a) Coastal Palms Franchise Holdings LLC** (\"Coastal Palms\" or \"CPFH\") --- a Florida limited liability company with its principal office at 9500 Gulf Shore Drive, Suite 450, Naples, Florida 34108. Coastal Palms\' registered agent is Garrison Registered Agents LLC, 100 S. Ashley Drive, Suite 600, Tampa, Florida 33602. Coastal Palms was, at the time of the filing of this action, Verimark\'s single largest franchise operator, holding franchise rights to twenty-two (22) hotel properties --- eighteen (18) operating under the Verimark Suites flag and four (4) operating under the Verimark Select flag --- located across Florida and Georgia, comprising approximately 3,740 total guest rooms.

**(b) Randall \"Randy\" Brecker** --- Managing Member and sixty percent (60%) equity holder of Coastal Palms. Mr. Brecker served as the day-to-day decision-maker for all Coastal Palms operations and was also the President of Suncoast Room Management Inc., the affiliated management company through which the revenue-diversion scheme was conducted.

**(c) Theresa Brecker** --- Member and fifteen percent (15%) equity holder of Coastal Palms. Ms. Brecker is the spouse of Randall Brecker. Her involvement in the day-to-day operations of Coastal Palms was limited, but she was a signatory on certain financial documents and loan agreements relevant to the litigation.

**(d) Nolan Prescott** --- Member and twenty-five percent (25%) equity holder of Coastal Palms. Mr. Prescott is a retired commercial real estate developer who served as a passive investor in Coastal Palms. His role was principally financial; he did not participate in day-to-day management but was a co-guarantor on several of the Ironclad National Bank mortgage loans and was a signatory on the operating agreement.

**(e) Gulf Breeze Hospitality LLC** --- a Florida limited liability company owning and operating six (6) Verimark Suites properties in Southwest Florida. Gulf Breeze Hospitality LLC was managed by Randall Brecker and functioned as a subsidiary or affiliate entity within the Coastal Palms organizational structure.

**(f) Savannah Lodging Partners LLC** --- a Georgia limited liability company owning and operating four (4) Verimark Suites properties in coastal Georgia (Savannah and Brunswick). Savannah Lodging Partners LLC was likewise managed by Randall Brecker.

**(g) Suncoast Room Management Inc.** --- a Florida corporation; an affiliated management company established by Randall Brecker no later than January 2013. Suncoast collected revenues from direct bookings --- including walk-in guests, corporate-direct contracts, and bookings made through the unbranded website gulfcoastrooms.com --- and retained a twelve percent (12%) \"management fee\" on those revenues. Neither Suncoast\'s gross collections nor the management fee were included in the Gross Room Revenue reports submitted to Verimark. Suncoast was the central vehicle through which the revenue-diversion scheme operated.

This matter involved a breach-of-contract action arising from Coastal Palms\' systematic underreporting of Gross Room Revenue (\"GRR\") over a nine-year period spanning 2013 through 2021. The underreporting resulted in the chronic and substantial underpayment of three categories of fees owed to Verimark under the parties\' Franchise License Agreements: (i) royalties, calculated at five percent (5%) of GRR pursuant to FLA § 4.1; (ii) marketing-fund contributions, calculated at two and one-half percent (2.5%) of GRR pursuant to FLA § 4.2; and (iii) technology fees, assessed at \$12.50 per available room per month, with consumer price index adjustments capped at three percent (3%) annually, pursuant to FLA § 4.3.

The revenue-diversion scheme at the heart of this dispute operated as follows: Beginning no later than January 2013, Coastal Palms, acting through and at the direction of Randall Brecker, established Suncoast Room Management Inc. as a nominally separate management company. Suncoast collected revenues from direct bookings --- a category encompassing walk-in guests paying at the front desk, corporate accounts that booked directly with the properties rather than through Verimark\'s centralized reservation system, and guests who booked through the unbranded website gulfcoastrooms.com, which Suncoast created and operated. Suncoast retained a twelve percent (12%) \"management fee\" on all revenues it collected. Critically, neither Suncoast\'s gross collections nor the management fee were included in the GRR figures that Coastal Palms reported to Verimark for purposes of calculating royalties, marketing-fund contributions, and technology fees.

In addition to the Suncoast-based diversion, Coastal Palms also systematically underreported revenue from third-party online travel agencies (\"OTAs\") by netting commissions paid to the OTAs against GRR before reporting it to Verimark. This netting practice violated the FLAs\' definition of GRR, which was defined on a gross basis without deduction for commissions, discounts, or fees paid to intermediaries.

The underreporting was estimated at between twenty-two percent (22%) and thirty-one percent (31%) of actual GRR across the portfolio, with variation by individual property and by year. The total underreported GRR over the nine-year period was estimated at approximately \$197.8 million. For fiscal year 2021 alone --- the year immediately preceding the discovery of the scheme --- Coastal Palms reported GRR of \$112.4 million, whereas estimated true GRR was \$145.6 million, representing an underreporting of approximately \$33.2 million for that single year.

The contractual relationship between Verimark and Coastal Palms was governed by twenty-two (22) individual Franchise License Agreements (\"FLAs\"), one for each franchised hotel property. The first FLA was executed on June 15, 2007, for the Naples property, and the most recent FLA was executed on September 3, 2019. Each FLA provided for a twenty (20)-year initial term and was governed by the laws of the State of Florida, with mandatory venue for any litigation in Broward County, Florida.
The following provisions of the FLAs were of central importance to the claims asserted in this matter:

> • **Section 4.1 --- Royalties:** Franchisee to pay Verimark a royalty equal to five percent (5%) of Gross Room Revenue, payable monthly, within fifteen (15) days following the end of each calendar month.

> • **Section 4.2 --- Marketing-Fund Contribution:** Franchisee to contribute two and one-half percent (2.5%) of Gross Room Revenue to the Verimark National Marketing Fund, payable concurrently with royalties.

> • **Section 4.3 --- Technology Fee:** Franchisee to pay a technology fee of \$12.50 per available room per month, subject to annual CPI adjustment capped at three percent (3%) per year, to support Verimark\'s centralized reservation system, property-management system integrations, and brand technology platforms.

> • **Section 8.2 --- Audit Rights:** Verimark entitled to audit franchisee\'s financial records upon ten (10) business days\' written notice. If an audit reveals an underpayment exceeding two percent (2%) of reported GRR for the audited period, the franchisee bears all audit costs.

> • **Section 15.3 --- Liquidated Damages upon Termination for Cause:** In the event of termination by Verimark for cause, the franchisee shall pay liquidated damages equal to three times (3×) the trailing-twelve-month royalties attributable to the terminated property.

These provisions collectively formed the legal framework upon which Verimark\'s claims were built and provided the contractual bases for the damages calculations set forth in Dr. Kettlewell\'s expert report.

The origins of this matter trace to a whistleblower complaint received by Verimark\'s compliance hotline. On **November 8, 2021**, Janet Kerrigan, a former regional controller for Coastal Palms who had been terminated in October 2021, contacted the Verimark compliance hotline and reported allegations of systematic revenue diversion by Coastal Palms and its affiliated entity, Suncoast Room Management Inc. Ms. Kerrigan alleged that Randall Brecker had directed property-level accounting staff to exclude direct-booking revenues collected by Suncoast from the GRR reports submitted to Verimark, and that this practice had been ongoing for several years.

On **November 15, 2021**, Calderwood & Harkness LLP, operating under a separate pre-engagement letter agreement with Verimark for advisory services, provided a preliminary analysis of the whistleblower allegations. Yuki Nakamura prepared a memorandum to Priya Anand assessing the legal implications of the allegations under the FLAs, the potential scope of damages, and the recommended investigative steps. The memorandum concluded that, if substantiated, the allegations described conduct that would constitute both a material breach and a potentially incurable breach under FLA § 14.2(c).

On **January 18, 2022**, Thornbury delivered its preliminary findings. The following key learnings and practice points are documented for the benefit of Calderwood & Harkness LLP\'s attorneys and for future matters involving similar issues.

The early and aggressive pursuit of Suncoast Room Management Inc.\'s financial records was critical to the successful prosecution of this matter. Suncoast was the vehicle through which the revenue-diversion scheme operated, and its records --- including bank statements, gulfcoastrooms.com booking logs, corporate-direct contract files, and internal accounting spreadsheets --- formed the backbone of the damages case. Without the 312,000 documents produced as a result of the Motion to Compel (filed September 15, 2022; granted October 28, 2022), it would have been extremely difficult to quantify the scope of the underreporting with the precision required for Dr. Kettlewell\'s expert report.

The lesson for future franchise-litigation matters is clear: when a franchisee uses affiliated entities to collect or divert revenue, counsel must move early and aggressively to compel production of those entities\' records, including through formal motion practice if necessary. Defense counsel will predictably resist production on the ground that the affiliate is a \"separate entity,\" and the discovery record should be developed with an eye toward establishing common control and alter-ego arguments.

The e-discovery protocol established by joint stipulation on June 20, 2022, facilitated efficient processing and review of the document universe. However, the volume of documents ultimately processed --- approximately 2.3 million documents comprising 1.1 terabytes --- substantially exceeded the initial estimates provided to Nexagen and drove e-discovery costs significantly above budget. Future matters of comparable complexity should incorporate more conservative initial volume estimates and establish tiered pricing structures with the e-discovery vendor to manage cost escalation.

Janet Kerrigan\'s whistleblower complaint to the Verimark compliance hotline on November 8, 2021, was the catalyst for the entire investigation and, ultimately, for this litigation. Without her complaint, the revenue-diversion scheme might have continued undetected for years. Her subsequent deposition testimony corroborated the documentary evidence of Randall Brecker\'s instructions to exclude direct-booking revenues from the GRR reports submitted to Verimark. Ms. Kerrigan\'s testimony was compelling, consistent with the documentary record, and would have been powerful trial evidence.

The lesson for future franchise matters is that franchisor clients should be advised to systematically cultivate and protect whistleblower relationships. This includes maintaining robust and accessible compliance hotlines, responding promptly and substantively to whistleblower reports, and ensuring that whistleblower protections --- including confidentiality of the whistleblower\'s identity to the extent practicable --- are observed throughout the investigation and litigation. Where a key witness is a former employee of the opposing party, early witness-preparation work and periodic contact to maintain the relationship are essential.

For future matters, where pre-litigation audit work is performed by a different firm than the retained litigation expert, engagement terms should be structured from the outset to facilitate coordination, and the preliminary audit engagement should be scoped with an awareness that its findings may become exhibits in subsequent litigation.

The Court\'s February 9, 2024 Order granting Verimark\'s Motion for Partial Summary Judgment on Counts I and II (liability only) was the decisive event that moved this case toward resolution. By establishing liability as a matter of law --- and, critically, by rejecting Coastal Palms\' GRR-ambiguity argument --- the Court eliminated Coastal Palms\' primary defense and left only the question of damages for trial. This fundamentally altered the settlement calculus for both parties.

Before the summary-judgment ruling, Coastal Palms maintained a negotiating posture anchored in its contention that the GRR definition was ambiguous and that a reasonable jury could find in its favor on liability. Once the Court ruled that the GRR definition was unambiguous and that Coastal Palms\' interpretation was untenable, the only remaining questions were the quantum of damages and the enforceability of the liquidated-damages provision --- questions on which Verimark held a strong, though not risk-free, position.

The investment in summary-judgment briefing --- which was substantial in both hours and effort --- was fully justified by the result. Future matters with strong contract-interpretation arguments should prioritize summary-judgment motions as a mechanism for establishing liability and driving settlement, particularly where the opposing party\'s primary defense rests on an arguably strained contract interpretation.

Ironclad National Bank\'s approximately \$94 million in first-lien mortgage loans on eighteen (18) of the twenty-two (22) Coastal Palms properties created significant collectibility risk that informed every aspect of the settlement analysis. Even a judgment of \$150 million would have been of limited value if Coastal Palms lacked unencumbered assets sufficient to satisfy the judgment. The Ironclad liens took priority over any judicial lien that Verimark could obtain, and forced liquidation of the properties through foreclosure or receivership would have been a protracted and uncertain process.

The settlement structure directly addressed this concern. The \$25 million cash payment at closing provided immediate, certain recovery. The security interest in eight (8) unencumbered hotel properties --- valued at \$71.2 million in the aggregate --- provides collateral support for the \$62.5 million in structured payments that is not subordinate to Ironclad\'s liens. The personal guaranties from Brecker and Prescott provide additional recovery backstops, although the individual net worth of each guarantor was not independently verified.

The lesson for future matters is that collectibility analysis must be conducted early in the litigation and revisited periodically. The availability (or unavailability) of unencumbered assets should drive both the settlement strategy and the structuring of any settlement consideration.

The franchise surrender of fourteen (14) properties, while not reflected as a dollar amount in the \$87.5 million headline settlement figure, represents significant strategic value to Verimark. The surrender removes a demonstrably non-compliant operator from a substantial portion of the Verimark brand network and frees those fourteen (14) locations for re-franchising to compliant operators or for strategic repositioning under the Verimark Grand or Verimark Select flags. The franchise-surrender component was, in many respects, as important to Verimark from a brand-protection perspective as the monetary recovery.

Additionally, the Enhanced Audit Protocol applicable to the eight (8) retained properties --- including quarterly audits, real-time POS integration, and franchisee-funded audit costs for five years --- provides Verimark with ongoing visibility into Coastal Palms\' revenue reporting that it did not previously have, substantially reducing the risk of future noncompliance.

The \$105.5 million liquidated-damages claim under FLA § 15.3 --- calculated as 3× trailing-twelve-month corrected royalties per property, across all twenty-two (22) properties --- was the single largest component of Verimark\'s claimed damages and the most significant source of uncertainty in the damages model. Under Florida law, a liquidated-damages provision is enforceable only if the stipulated amount is a reasonable forecast of just compensation for the harm caused by the breach and the harm is of a kind that is difficult or impossible to accurately estimate at the time of contracting. *See Lefemine v. Baron*, 573 So. 2d 326 (Fla. 1991). A liquidated-damages provision that functions as a penalty --- rather than a reasonable pre-estimate of loss --- is unenforceable.

The 3× multiplier applied across all twenty-two (22) properties created a meaningful risk that a court would find the aggregate liquidated damages of \$105.5 million to be disproportionate to the actual harm suffered, particularly given that the direct underpayments (royalties, marketing contributions, and technology fees) totaled only \$16.095 million. While there were strong arguments that the liquidated-damages provision was enforceable --- including the difficulty of quantifying the downstream harm to the Verimark brand from a franchisee\'s systematic revenue diversion --- the risk of a finding that the provision constituted an unenforceable penalty was a key factor in the settlement calculus.

Had the liquidated-damages claim been struck, Verimark\'s remaining damages would have consisted of the \$16.095 million in direct underpayments and the \$28.4 million in contractual late-payment interest, for a total of approximately \$44.5 million --- well below the \$87.5 million settlement. The settlement effectively captures the value of the liquidated-damages claim at a significant discount, while eliminating the binary trial risk that the claim might be rejected entirely.

Reference is made to the Post-Settlement Compliance Monitoring Memorandum dated April 26, 2024, prepared by Yuki Nakamura and transmitted to Renata Solis-Vega and Deidre Langston at Verimark. That memorandum provides detailed monitoring protocols and timelines for each post-settlement obligation. The following is a summary of the key monitoring items:

> The fourteen (14) surrendered properties must be de-identified --- with all Verimark branding, signage, proprietary systems, and technology integrations removed --- by **August 20, 2024** (120 days from the April 22, 2024 execution date). Deidre Langston\'s franchise operations team will monitor compliance with the de-identification requirements.

> The eight (8) retained properties are to operate under new ten (10)-year Franchise License Agreements incorporating the Enhanced Audit Protocol (quarterly audits, real-time POS integration, franchisee-funded audit costs for five years). Execution and delivery of the new FLAs is to be completed in connection with the settlement closing.

> The UCC-1 Financing Statement filed with the Florida Secured Transaction Registry should be periodically reviewed to ensure continued perfection of Verimark\'s first-priority security interest in the eight (8) unencumbered hotel properties. Continuation statements should be filed prior to the five-year lapse period, as applicable.

> Any missed or late structured payment triggers potential acceleration of the entire outstanding balance under the Settlement Agreement\'s default and acceleration provisions. Verimark\'s legal department should establish calendaring and tracking procedures to ensure timely identification of any payment defaults.

**Ongoing Advisory Role:** Verimark\'s in-house legal team (Renata Solis-Vega and Deidre Langston) will handle routine monitoring of all post-settlement obligations. Calderwood & Harkness LLP remains available on an as-needed advisory basis for enforcement actions, default proceedings, or any disputes arising under the Settlement Agreement or the new FLAs.

{"file_path":"response.md","content":"# Largest settlement identified

## Answer

The largest settlement in the firm’s matter files is **$87,500,000** in **_Verimark Hospitality Group Inc. v. Coastal Palms Franchise Holdings LLC, et al._, Case No. 1021-00006**, in the Circuit Court of the Seventeenth Judicial Circuit in and for Broward County, Florida.

The client was **Verimark Hospitality Group Inc.** The opposing parties were Coastal Palms Franchise Holdings LLC and related Coastal Palms parties, including Randall Brecker, Theresa Brecker, Nolan Prescott, Gulf Breeze Hospitality LLC, Savannah Lodging Partners LLC, and Suncoast Room Management Inc.

## Why $87.5 million is the correct number

The executed settlement agreement defines the **“Settlement Amount”** as **“the aggregate sum of Eighty-Seven Million Five Hundred Thousand Dollars ($87,500,000)”**. Its operative payment provision likewise states that the Coastal Palms parties must pay Verimark a total Settlement Amount of $87.5 million in full and final settlement of the claims and counterclaims.

The agreement breaks that amount into:

- **$25,000,000** initial payment at closing; and
- **$62,500,000** in eight structured payments of **$7,812,500** each.

Those components total **$87,500,000**. I did **not** add the agreement’s separate 6.5% interest on the structured payments, because the agreement defines the settlement amount as the $87.5 million principal amount. I also did not add the approximately **$71.2 million** appraised value of collateral, the value of the franchise surrender and enhanced audit rights, or Verimark’s approximately **$150 million** damages claim. Those are, respectively, financing/security, non-cash settlement value, and claimed-damages figures—not the settlement amount defined by the executed agreement.

The agreement was executed/effective **April 22, 2024**. Its signature pages are dated April 22, 2024 for Verimark, Coastal Palms, the individual parties, the related entities, and counsel. The firm’s closing memorandum records the matter’s final disposition and separately describes the total settlement as **$87.5 million**, noting that it represented approximately 58.3% of Verimark’s approximately $150 million damages claim.

## Comparison and review method

I reviewed the settlement-related materials and compared the aggregate monetary amount defined in final or execution-version settlement agreements, rather than relying on drafts, term sheets, settlement authority, offers, claimed damages, or collateral values. As a cross-check on the high end of the range:

| Matter | Executed/final agreement amount | Source |
|---|---:|---|
| _Verimark Hospitality Group Inc. v. Coastal Palms Franchise Holdings LLC, et al._, Case No. 1021-00006 | **$87,500,000** | Final Settlement Agreement and Mutual Release, § 1.22 and § 2.1 |
| _Verimark Hospitality Group Inc. v. Ironclad Indemnity Corporation, et al._, Case No. 1021-00003 | $47,300,000 | Settlement Agreement and Mutual Release, § 1.1(l) and § 2.1 |
| Matter 1033-00006, _RGC_ action | $14,750,000 | Settlement Agreement—Execution, § 1(o) and § 2.1 |
| Matter 1038-00007, _Vantor_ action | $14,750,000 | Settlement Agreement and Mutual Release, § 1.6 and § 2.1 |
| Matter 1017-00004 class action | $14,750,000 gross settlement amount | Class Settlement Agreement—Execution, § 1.13 |
| Matter 1034-00002 family litigation settlement | $14,500,000 lump-sum cash payment | Settlement Agreement/Stipulation, § 4.2 |

The $47.3 million settlement in Matter 1021-00003 is the next-largest executed settlement identified in the review, so it does not displace the $87.5 million Verimark/Coastal Palms settlement.

## Matters/documents relied on

1. **Matter 1021-00006 — _Verimark Hospitality Group Inc. v. Coastal Palms Franchise Holdings LLC, et al._**
   - `documents/matters/1021-00006/Mediation & Settlement/final-settlement-agreement-execution.docx`
     - Caption and case number: opening page.
     - Execution/effective date: April 22, 2024.
     - Defined **Settlement Amount**: § 1.22.
     - Total settlement and payment components: §§ 2.1–2.3.
     - Executed signature pages: dated April 22, 2024.
   - `documents/matters/1021-00006/Client Reporting/matter-closing-memorandum.docx`
     - Identifies the matter and client.
     - Records the final disposition and states that the total settlement was $87.5 million.
     - Explains that the $87.5 million was distinct from the approximately $150 million claim, the non-cash franchise rights, and the collateral supporting the structured payments.

2. **Matter 1021-00003 — _Verimark Hospitality Group Inc. v. Ironclad Indemnity Corporation, Pinnacle Surplus Lines Inc., Montclair Assurance Company, and Sovereign Re Ltd._**
   - `documents/matters/1021-00003/Mediation & Settlement/settlement-agreement-mutual-release.docx`
     - Effective date: December 19, 2023.
     - Defined aggregate Settlement Amount: $47.3 million.
     - Used as the principal high-end comparison.

3. **Additional high-value executed settlement agreements used for the cross-check**
   - `documents/matters/1033-00006/Settlement Documents/settlement-agreement-execution.docx` — $14.75 million.
   - `documents/matters/1038-00007/Settlement/settlement-agreement-mutual-release.docx` — $14.75 million.
   - `documents/matters/1017-00004/Mediation & Settlement/Class Action/class-settlement-agreement-execution.docx` — $14.75 million gross settlement amount.
   - `documents/matters/1034-00002/Settlement/settlement-agreement-stipulation.docx` — $14.5 million lump-sum cash payment.

**Bottom line for the pitch:** the defensible headline is **“$87.5 million settlement achieved for Verimark Hospitality Group in _Verimark v. Coastal Palms_, Case No. 1021-00006.”**"}
